subject: Astronomy & Space
title: The Radial Velocity Method
description: A 60-second lesson on The Radial Velocity Method.

hook.text: A planet's gravity tugs on its star, making the star wobble. That wobble shifts the star's light in a detectable way.

buildup.text: As the star moves toward us, its light shifts blue. As it moves away, it shifts red. This is the Doppler effect.

discovery.text: Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz used this method to find 51 Pegasi b in 1995—earning them a Nobel Prize in 2019.

twist.text: This method reveals a planet's mass and orbit but not its size. It's complementary to the transit method.

climax.text: Modern spectrographs can detect star wobbles of just 1 m/s—a slow walking speed from light-years away.

punchline.text: Stars wobble when planets pull. That wobble crosses the galaxy to reach our instruments.

quiz.question: What does the radial velocity method measure to find exoplanets?
options: The wobble of a star caused by a planet's gravitational pull
The speed at which a planet orbits its star
Changes in a star's brightness over time

details.summary: The radial velocity method detects exoplanets by measuring tiny Doppler shifts in a star's spectrum caused by the gravitational tug of an orbiting planet. As the planet orbits, the star wobbles toward and away from us, shifting its light between blue and red.
details.whyItMatters: The radial velocity method provides planet masses — complementing the transit method's size measurements. Together they determine planet density, revealing whether a world is rocky, gassy, or icy.
takeaways: Measures the star's wobble caused by an orbiting planet
Detects Doppler shifts in the star's light spectrum
Provides planet mass, complementing transit-based size data

faq.question: How sensitive is the radial velocity method?
faq.answer: Modern spectrographs like ESPRESSO can detect stellar wobbles as small as 10 cm/s — Earth induces a wobble of about 9 cm/s on the Sun. Detecting Earth-mass planets in the habitable zone of Sun-like stars is at the very edge of current capability but improving steadily.

faq.question: What are the method's limitations?
faq.answer: It measures only the minimum mass (actual mass depends on orbital inclination). Stellar activity like starspots can mimic planet signals. It works best for massive planets close to their star and is biased toward detecting larger short-period planets rather than small, distant ones.
